narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.5% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. You placed in the third decile, noticeably lower than the average of accepted students (around the sixth decile). This single piece of information had the largest impact on the outcome.

Your first-year ranking worked in the opposite direction. Placing in the fifth decile was better than many accepted applicants and helped pull the prediction back toward passing, but not enough to overcome the later dip in performance.

Your family’s upper-middle income bracket also nudged the model slightly toward predicting failure. While this is the most common income group among accepted students (45%), the model still interpreted it as a modest risk factor compared with higher-income backgrounds.

Taken together, these pieces of your profile led the system to conclude you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your academic performance in later years and consider additional bar-preparation resources that can demonstrate your readiness. Improving your class rank and supplementing your record with strong practice-exam results could meaningfully change how a similar model evaluates you next time. (248 words)
